source_title: Ghar ka khana is the best: Why Dr SK Sarin wants Indians to rethink their daily diet - India Today
source_excerpt:
Dr SK Sarin urged Indians to prioritise home-cooked meals over dietary supplements. His advice stressed balanced diets, familiar foods and sustainable everyday choices.
A healthier life may not begin with an expensive supplement, a protein powder or the latest wellness trend. It may begin in your kitchen, with a plate of ghar ka khana.
That was the message from Dr SK Sarin, Director of the Institute of Liver and Biliary Sciences (ILBS), New Delhi, at the India Today HealthWealth Summit. Speaking during the session Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara , Sarin urged people to focus on what they eat every day rather than depend on supplements to make up for poor dietary choices.
“Homemade food is the best. Outside food should be eaten only sometimes,” he said.
His advice brought the focus back to familiar Indian foods, including buttermilk, sattu and green vegetables, while raising questions about the growing reliance on supplements and packaged health products.
For Sarin, eating well is not about following the latest diet trend. It is about building a sustainable routine around nutritious food, appropriate portions and healthier everyday choices. WHY GHAR KA KHANA SHOULD COME FIRST
The appeal of home-cooked food goes beyond nostalgia. Preparing meals at home makes it easier to control the ingredients, cooking methods, salt, sugar and the amount of fat used.
Sarin's central message was clear: “Don't use supplements with poor-quality food.” Supplements have become increasingly popular, with products marketed for everything from sleep and energy to skin health and muscle recovery. But they cannot replace a balanced diet or compensate for consistently poor eating habits.
“Never take a supplement in isolation. Take it with food,” Sarin said.
The first step, Sarin believes, is to assess the quality of the diet rather than assume that a supplement can fill every nutritional gap.
He singled out buttermilk, sattu and green vegetables while discussing healthier food choices. Buttermilk can be a useful addition to meals. Sattu is another traditional Indian food that offers protein and dietary fibre.
It can be consumed in different forms, including a savoury drink or as part of a meal. Eating a variety of vegetables regularly can help improve overall diet quality.
These foods are not miracle cures, nor does any single ingredient guarantee good health. Their value lies in how they fit into a varied and balanced diet.
Sarin also discussed the nutritional potential of buttermilk, referring to data on the subject being presented at a conference in the United States.
His broader point was to pay attention to familiar foods that can form part of a healthy daily eating pattern instead of assuming that better health requires expensive products. - Ends
